author: William Saville

title: The Listening Fair
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fourth expansion pass
content:
Toph did not like the name of the Listening Fair.

"Sounds like a competition for people with ears," she said.

Greg laughed.

"Well, technically—"

"Finish that sentence and I'll make you eat your guitar."

I tried very hard to look professional.

The fair was a small event at Starwake Pier, arranged to raise money for repairing the western boardwalk and teaching people how to recognize the sounds of an unsafe structure. It wasn't a concert, though Greg had offered music. Toph had agreed to demonstrate how she sensed movement through the earth and stone. Iroh was bringing tea and a few simple percussion instruments for visitors who wanted to join in.

The trouble was that everyone had a different idea of what listening meant.

Greg wanted people to hear how a melody changed when it made room for another sound. Toph wanted them to pay attention to the floor beneath their feet. Iroh wanted people to notice what was happening before they decided how to respond.

I wanted them to stop arguing over the program.

"Why don't we ask the people coming?" I said.

Toph folded her arms.

"Because they haven't come yet."

"Then maybe we should stop pretending we know what they'll need."

Greg grinned.

"That's a pretty good lyric."

"Don't."

He laughed.

We set up three stations along the safe section of the pier. The first had a low table of wooden objects that made different sounds when tapped. The second had a practice platform where Toph could demonstrate vibration without anyone walking onto the damaged western boards. The third was a small listening circle, with chairs arranged so people could choose whether to participate or simply sit.

Iroh placed a kettle near the entrance.

"That is a great deal of noise for a listening fair," he observed.

"Thank you," Toph said. "Finally, someone sensible."

He smiled.

"Perhaps the noise will teach us what quiet can offer."

Toph groaned.

"Never mind."

By noon the fair had begun.

A child from the square discovered that a hollow wooden block made a deep note while a smaller solid one clicked sharply. An older visitor tapped a cup and asked why the sound changed when it was filled with water. Iroh explained the vibration of the vessel without turning the answer into a lecture about life.

Greg watched the small group with interest.

"Can I try something?" he asked.

Toph tilted her head.

"Depends."

He played three quiet notes on his guitar, then stopped.

The sound faded into the air.

"Now," he said, "what did you hear after the last note?"

At first nobody answered.

Then Edda pointed toward the far railing.

"The wind through the gaps."

Pip said they heard the water under the boards.

A child said they heard someone laughing by the tea stand.

Greg smiled.

"Exactly."

Toph looked toward him.

"That was actually good."

He blinked.

"Thanks?"

"Don't get used to it."

I watched them grin at each other and felt the strange pleasure of seeing people I cared about find a way to work together without having to become the same person.

At the practice platform, Toph explained how she could sense small changes through the stone beneath her feet. She did not claim to hear every sound or know every danger.

"Earth tells me some things," she said. "Wood tells me less. And if you need to know whether a railing is safe, you still check it with proper tools."

Danse, who had come to supervise the temporary supports, nodded.

"Correct."

Toph smirked.

"Write that down, tin man."

He looked as though he wanted to object.

Then he smiled.

Iroh watched the exchange over his cup.

"Learning to listen can make even a disagreement useful."

"Don't put that on a sign," Toph said.

"Too late," Greg whispered to me.

He had already written it in his notebook.

The afternoon was not perfect. One guest demanded that Greg play the old grief-song he'd refused at the Lantern Walk. Greg said no and offered another piece. The guest left disappointed. Nobody chased them.

Another visitor wanted Toph to demonstrate her abilities by breaking a stone wall. She declined because the point of the fair was noticing damage before someone got hurt, not creating new damage for entertainment.

Iroh had to close the tea station early when the last kettle emptied.

No one could conjure more water from politeness.

The fair ended with a small group sitting by the repaired railings. Greg played a slow melody. Iroh tapped a gentle rhythm on the rim of a wooden cup. Toph placed one hand on the safe stone platform and followed the beat through her fingers.

For a while they matched each other.

Then Greg stopped playing.

The rhythm continued, soft and uneven, carried by Iroh's cup and the sound of people shifting in their chairs. The water beneath the pier made its own quiet music.

Greg looked at me.

"That's what I was trying to write."

I smiled.

"The part where you stop?"

"The part where stopping doesn't mean the song's over."

I felt a small ache of affection.

Afterward we counted the donations. The fair had raised enough for new fasteners and part of the boardwalk lumber, but not the entire repair. We wrote the amount clearly on the notice board. Tamsin would order only what the fund could cover, and the damaged area would stay closed until the remaining money was found.

Greg set down his guitar.

"I think that was worth doing."

"It was," I said.

He looked at the empty chairs.

"Even though nobody got a big show?"

"Especially then."

He laughed.

Iroh packed the cups, Toph collected her practice stones, and the volunteers signed off on the cleanup rota. Nobody disappeared before putting away the equipment they'd agreed to carry.

When the pier was finally quiet, Greg and I stood by the water.

"How was I?" he asked.

"Very talented."

"Only talented?"

"Annoyingly talented."

He grinned.

"That's better."

Then he grew serious.

"Thanks for not pushing me to play something I wasn't ready to play."

"You get to decide what your songs mean."

He nodded.

I took his hand.

The evening air was cool, and the last light had turned the water silver. He leaned close enough that I could smell the faint scent of guitar strings and salt on his clothes.

"May I kiss you?" he asked.

"Yes."

His kiss was warm, gentle, and a little shy. We stayed by the railing until the first lanterns came on, listening to the sounds the fair had taught us not to overlook.

The pier still needed work.

So did we, sometimes.

But I liked the quiet between the notes.
